names.name: Śiva / Ādinātha, the guru whose nature is nāda, bindu and kalā
nirañjana, the stainless; paraṃ padam, the supreme state
parameśvara, the formless end of the tattvas
the one eternal knowledge without beginning or end (Śiva Saṃhitā 1.1)
Brahman as being, consciousness and bliss; the world full of Viṣṇu (Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā 7.4, 7.18)

descriptions: Whatever is heard as nāda is śakti; the formless end of the tattvas is the supreme Lord; the soundless is the supreme Brahman (HYP 4.101–102).
Stainless, unmoving, eternal, actionless, qualityless, great, consciousness of space, bliss (GŚ 99).
The supreme abode of Viṣṇu, where the mind dissolves within the resonance of the unstruck sound (HYP 4.100).
negations: nirātaṅka, nirālamba, niṣprapañca, nirāśraya, nirāmaya, nirākāra (GŚ 92)
not smell, taste, form, touch or sound; neither self nor other (HYP 4.109)
relation_to_self: In samādhi the individual self and the supreme self become one, as salt dissolves in water (HYP 4.5–7); 'I am Brahman and no other' (GS 7.4).
relation_to_world: Duality is only what the mind sees; through unmanī it is not perceived (HYP 4.61); the world is the play of māyā (SS 1.64–67) — for the Vedāntic haṭha texts. The body is a microcosm of the world (SS 2.1–5).
caveat: The haṭha texts are practice manuals whose metaphysics is borrowed: Advaita in HYP 4 and Śiva Saṃhitā 1, a Vaiṣṇava theism joined to Advaita in the Gheraṇḍa, Śaiva in the Khecarīvidyā, Buddhist tantric in the Amṛtasiddhi. The HYP itself says of laya 'let this be called liberation or not' (4.30, 4.78), subordinating doctrine to attained state. The Amṛtasiddhi's Buddhist setting would not accept a Brahman–ātman reading of the one truth; the Amanaska subordinates all methods to the mindless state rather than to a named ultimate.
